messages.author: dc06d729e023580a
messages.subject: ggplot2 development update
parts:
Hi everyone,

As you may have noticed, ggplot2 development has slid to a grinding
halt recently, so I wanted to reaffirm my long-term commitment to
ggplot2, and let you know what I'm doing to make development easier in
the future. Unfortunately, for the short term, I've had to give up on
my long-promised layout rewrite - because the code is so complex, I
need a large amount of time to dedicate to it, and because it has no
tests, the probability of creating an undetected bug is high. Instead,
I'm working on something a little more modest, but more achievable,
and will have much bigger long term benefits. I'm now focussing on
extracting core components of ggplot2 out into their own packages.
This, I hope, will have a number of advantages:

* The new packages will be written using what I know about
developing packages, and will substantially easier for others to
understand. This should make it easier for interested community
members to start contributing, without having to wade through the
extremely complicated code of ggplot2. The new packages will also
include tests that will make it easier for me (and others) to make
improvements without introducing new bugs.

* Because the packages will implement things that all graphics
packages need, I hope that other graphics package authors will
contribute, and provide pieces that ggplot2 lacks. Also, I'll be able
to use the packages in my current research efforts (interactive
graphics) so I'll have added incentive to work on them.

* As more ggplot2 components migrate into their own packages, the
core of ggplot2 will become much simpler, and it will be much easier
to make bigger, structural changes.

So far I've started this process for two components of ggplot2:

* scales and guides: https://github.com/hadley/scales
* binning in 1d and 2d: https://github.com/hadley/bin

This process has already paid off by freeing me to aggressively
rewrite much of the code, focussing on reducing duplication and a
simpler API. This will eventually pay off by making it possible to
create a new ggplot2 scale in just a line or two of code. (It also
means you can use ggplot2 scales in base graphics if you want). Other
natural candidates for this process include coordinate systems,
position adjustments, fortify, and perhaps some part geoms and stats.
(If you'd like to work on any of these, let me know! I'd be very happy
to mentor you and it would be a great way to learn how to make an R
package)

I'm also going to try and find funding for a ggplot2 programmer or
postdoc who could work on ggplot2 full time for a year or two.
Unfortunately this is quite a lot of money, so it's not going to be
easy, but the pay off would be huge.

Finally, if anyone is interested in spending a summer improving
ggplot2, I can almost guarantee funding for it.

Hadley
